extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature — scientists, academics, professional practitioners (including inventors and educators)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards used in Nature's book-reviews and notices for judging scientific and technical books (coverage, accuracy, style, practical usefulness, illustrations, legal/procedural treatment). Relevant for reviewers and authors preparing works for a scientific audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage/Completeness of subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A work on experimental zoology (or similar scientific treatise) should include the principal departments of the subject — e.g. regeneration, experimental embryology, and morphogenesis — and omission of such parts is 'especially regrettable' and diminishes completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Missing parts that are 'absolutely necessary to completeness' should be included in subsequent editions; a treatise titled 'Experimental Zoology' ought to cover both morphogenesis and the experimental work that illuminates the daily life of organisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centrality of morphogenesis
rubrics_metrics.description: The central problem of morphology is morphogenesis and a treatise on experimental zoology should give this problem central consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and reviewers should judge whether morphogenesis is treated as the central problem rather than sidelined by other topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of experimental approaches across related fields
rubrics_metrics.description: A comprehensive experimental zoology should include not only experiments on morphogenesis but also comparative physiology and psychology and other experimental work that helps understand the fully formed creature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad experimental approaches (regeneration, physiology, psychology) are essential for an all-round outlook and should not be excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author's competence and execution (workmanship)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author's competence is reflected in workmanship marked by carefulness, lucidity, impartiality, good-tempered criticism, and stimulating suggestion throughout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate clarity of exposition, fairness of critique, evidence of care in presentation, and whether the book stimulates further work or thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of author's aim and prescribed limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A book should be received with due consideration of the author's aim and prescribed limits; evaluation must take scope and stated intentions into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should distinguish between defects arising from poor execution and those due to deliberate scope-limitation by the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and accessibility for general/readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Works intended for broader audiences should be made clear and understandable without unnecessary technical apparatus (e.g. 'made clear without the use of mathematics'; 'style which everyone can understand').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether difficult subjects are presented in an accessible manner appropriate to the intended readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical usefulness for inventors/readers
rubrics_metrics.description: A guide to patent law should give inventors an explanation of the law and rules and information on protecting inventions, but an ordinary inventor may still have difficulty in drafting a specification from a short guide alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the book provides usable, practical advice for practitioners and where it falls short (e.g. drafting specifications) and whether it appropriately signals limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient legal depth and need for reference to larger works
rubrics_metrics.description: In a short work it is 'impossible' to give a full account of patent law; complex distinctions (e.g. patentable vs non-patentable inventions) often require fuller treatment and case law; every particular case must be judged on its merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short guides should signpost readers to larger, more detailed works and case law for nuanced legal questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of statutory text and indexing
rubrics_metrics.description: Useful legal guides should include the full statutory material (e.g. Patents Act, 1902, 'fully set out') and provide a fairly complete index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for reproduction of relevant statutes/rules and presence of a helpful index to aid practitioners and students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of controversial points and explanation of new practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A valuable account 'gives the effect of the new provisions very clearly' and 'very fully dealt with' controversial points (e.g. post-dating the specification, meaning of 'in part described', compulsory insertion of references).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess clarity in explaining recent changes, controversial interpretations, and procedural consequences for practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical procedural guidance on Patent Office powers
rubrics_metrics.description: A guide should explain Patent Office powers in practice (e.g. comptroller's power to post-date applications, how references may be required/inserted and in what form) and the practical convenience or hardship these may produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the book explains how procedural powers are likely to be exercised and their practical effect for applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensiveness of everyday-life / applied topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Works on practical life/health (e.g. 'The Efficient Life') should deal with nearly every phase of daily life — food, drink, fatigue, sleep, exercise, baths, physiological states — and propose artificial devices/strategies to ameliorate modern urban life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the book covers the range of relevant topics and whether its prescriptions are practical and likely to be beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for intended audience (amateur vs specialist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editions should be adapted to their intended readers (e.g. 'adapted to the use of amateur collectors of flowers'); revision should preserve features that made earlier editions useful to that audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether revisions improve or degrade usability for the target audience (e.g. amateurs vs botanists).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and quantity of illustrations and plates
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations (coloured plates, cuts) should be of good reproduction quality and adequate in size and number; reductions or poor drawings ('scrappy and attenuated') are a fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate image reproduction quality, completeness of illustrative material, and whether visual aids support identification/understanding as intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of taxonomic assignments and editorial proofreading
rubrics_metrics.description: Text must be accurate in botanical/taxonomic assignments (e.g. correct family/generic placements) and free from mistakes in words and nomenclature ('mistakes such as "aureole", "Hiberna", "paralias" are not infrequent').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check taxonomic decisions, nomenclature, and for typographical or editorial errors that could mislead readers; such errors degrade authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical production and format considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in physical size and bulk (e.g. increase in size/bulk of volume) and elimination of helpful layout features (e.g. guiding headlines under large genera) affect usability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether format/typography/layout changes aid or hinder the user's ability to consult the work efficiently.
